newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl's CDU delays decision on Bluem pensions plan.
newsitem.headline: Kohl's CDU delays decision on Bluem pensions plan.

text.p: Labour Minister Norbert Bluem's plan to reform German pensions hit resistance from fellow Christian Democrats (CDU) on Wednesday, forcing Chancellor Helmut Kohl to call more party talks on the issue.
The CDU party executive accepted some of Bluem's proposals, but in a rebuff for the embattled minister, CDU general secretary Peter Hintze did not rule out alternatives being floated.

Saxony state premier Kurt Biedenkopf, a senior party figure with a strong track record on pensions policy, told reporters that Bluem's plan was based on "unrealistic assumptions". He said he would be drafting his own counter-proposals.
"The plans cannot secure confidence in either the future of our pensions or in restoring growth and jobs," Biedenkopf said.

Bluem's plans to cut pensions, raise contributions and launch a tax-financed "family fund" to keep the pensions system working into the 21st century have aroused criticism from party colleagues, who were not consulted in the drafting process.
Bluem, Kohl's longest-serving minister, even clashed last weekend with his long-time boss. But Hintze said there was no hint of animosity between the two at the meeting.
"The discussions were businesslike," he told reporters.
Hintze said Bluem's proposal to reduce pensions to cope with the greying of the German population had met with the full support of CDU leaders.
A majority also backed limiting contributions to contain Germany's notoriously high labour overheads and trying to keep down state spending, Hintze said.
But party sources said that, in tough talks, fears emerged that the plans might inflate Germany's already bloated welfare state and put an unfair burden on the young.

It was not clear whether Bluem's model of cutting pensions to 64 percent of average net wages by 2030 from 70 percent now was likely to be accepted. He also wants contributions to rise to 22.9 percent from 20.3 percent -- already a record.

The pensions delay is also likely to hamper work on Finance Minister Theo Waigel's package of income and corporate tax cuts which would reduce the overall tax burden by 30 billion marks a year from 1999.

Waigel, by involving all three partners in Kohl's 14-year-old coalition in the policy process, has already done the hard work. Bluem, by only working with policy experts and bureaucrats, still has all the coalition horse-trading ahead.
Worse still, Bluem's demand for a rise in value-added tax to pay for the family fund, covering non-pensions items, runs headlong against Waigel's tax-cutting plans.

Hintze said a final CDU line on pensions may not be agreed until mid-March. That means that the idea of cross-party talks with the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) on pensions reform will have to be put on ice.

The SPD backed off from earlier offers of cooperation with the CDU on pensions, saying that Kohl's call on Tuesday for a "broad consensus" could not be taken seriously as long as the chancellor could not restore order in his own ranks.
And Lower Saxony state premier Gerhard Schroeder, one SPD leader who has kept his distance from the pensions debate, said the best solution would be for Kohl to call snap elections.
"Quick elections would be the cleanest solution to the government crisis. We are ready," he told the Wirtschaftswoche weekly.
Schroeder is seen as a likely challenger to SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine for the chancellorship at elections which are due by autumn 1998.
-- Bonn newsroom, 49-228-26097150
